methodology.record_unit: Distinct reusable claim/action/project/calculation or coherent procedure; related construction steps are grouped; individual jurisdiction claims are separate.

classifications.verified_guidance: Limited reviewed guidance independently supported by listed authoritative or product-primary evidence. Does not validate full book or installation.

classifications.needs_review: Conflicting, misleading, unsafe, incomplete or consequential unverified claim; do not promote to executable guidance.

limitations: This is a completed chapter-by-chapter source examination, not certification that every book claim is correct or every design can be built safely. All 82 pages were text-reviewed; 13 selected pages were visually inspected, including diagrams and high-risk claims. The other figures were not individually engineering-audited.

Records are distinct reusable claims, actions, calculations, projects or procedure units. Steps within one coherent procedure are grouped; alternative projects and individual state-law claims are separate. Counts depend on this declared granularity and are not a count of sentences or approved household tasks.
Twenty evidence sources were read through the web tool on the review date. URLs and section locators are retained; immutable copies of external pages were not archived. Web pages and laws can change.

Only the limited reviewed guidance of records classified verified_guidance is supported. A citation attached to a source-derived or needs-review record is context or a constraint, not validation of that book design.

The 28 non-Virginia state entries were preserved individually but not legally verified. Virginia guidance is statewide and does not determine locality-specific approval, permit applicability, property restrictions or financial eligibility.

Tax credits, product prices, performance and yield anecdotes, regional climate averages, author credentials, historic reservoir levels and many geopolitical claims remain unverified; narrative motivation was grouped as context rather than made into household actions.

No household size, parcel, location within Virginia, water test results, roof dimensions, measured demand or existing HomePrep taxonomy was available. Topic and milestone mappings are proposed library vocabulary, not existing app identifiers, capacity guarantees or completed milestones.

Neither homemade filter removal rates, carbon activation, pump prototype, well kits, fog harvest, dehumidifier potability, shower structures nor improvised repairs were laboratory-tested or professionally designed in this examination.

Original claims are paraphrased, with inclusive printed and PDF page ranges. Printed page number = one-based PDF page minus one throughout this edition. Grouped multi-page procedures retain their source span; paragraph coordinates are not supplied.

No HomePrep application files, imports or deployment were created or changed. All execution_eligible fields are false pending later content and implementation review. Book 2 is outside this examination.

record.title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply
record.locator: How much; Choosing a container; Cleaning; Storing; Using
record.finding: Emergency baseline: at least one gallon/person/day for three days; aim for two weeks and allow additional needs. Use suitable food-grade containers, never former toxic-chemical containers. Wash, sanitize with one teaspoon of 5-9% bleach per quart, wet all surfaces for 30 seconds, empty and air-dry. Fill with safe water, close tightly, date and keep cool, shaded and away from chemicals; replace home-filled water six-monthly. Handle hygienically. Unopened commercial water is a reliable emergency choice.

record.title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency
record.locator: Overview; Boil; Disinfect; Filtering; Using light
record.finding: Boiling clear water for one minute, or three above 6,500 feet, is the standard germ-control method. Let cloudy water settle or prefilter it. Bleach needs at least 30 minutes and concentration-specific dosing. Disinfectants are less effective for some parasites. Boiling and disinfection do not remove toxic chemicals. Ordinary filters may not remove all germs. Iodine is unsuitable for certain groups and extended use. Safe water is needed for food, dishes, teeth and hygiene.

record.title: How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency
record.locator: Inside the home; Outside the home
record.finding: Pool/spa water may serve hygiene and cleaning but is not drinking water. Outdoor sources can contain pathogens and chemicals; assess and treat them. Avoid fuel- or toxic-chemical-contaminated water for drinking and bathing.

record.title: About Choosing Home Water Filters
record.locator: Many filters do not remove germs; Do not rely on taste or smell; Test; Understand pore size
record.finding: Match treatment to tested contaminants and certified performance; ordinary carbon taste filters generally do not remove germs. Appearance and flavor do not prove safety. Test private well/rain supplies and follow system maintenance. Absolute and nominal pore ratings differ.

record.title: About Home Water Treatment Systems
record.locator: Reverse osmosis; Distillation
record.finding: RO and distillation can remove many germs and dissolved contaminants, but removal is system- and contaminant-specific. Distillation fails to remove some volatile compounds, solvents and pesticides. Treatment choice should follow water testing.

record.title: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
record.locator: Bleach table; Other Disinfection Methods
record.finding: For clear water EPA lists eight drops of 6% or six drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon, doubled for cloudy, colored or very cold water; wait 30 minutes, repeat if no slight chlorine odor then wait 15 more. Use fresh plain suitable bleach. HTH stock: heaping teaspoon in two gallons, then 1:100 (one pint per 12.5 gallons), with ventilation and eye protection. 2% iodine: five drops/quart clear or ten cloudy; wait 30 minutes. Tablets follow labels. These methods do not remove dissolved chemicals.

record.title: Order WaterBOB: instructions and FAQ
record.locator: Description; FAQ; Instructions
record.finding: Manufacturer recommends one-time use. Capacity is up to 100 gallons, limited by tub; do not fill above its rim. Tub is recommended for spill containment and convenience; manufacturer says the bladder can support itself. Instructions describe unfolding, faucet filling and dispensing with included pump. Storage claims are conditional, and the FAQ contains inconsistent four- and sixteen-week language; no duration guarantee is adopted here.

record.title: Collecting Rainwater and Your Health
record.locator: Health risks; Recommendations; Improve your system
record.finding: Rain may contain germs and chemicals from air, roofs and collection materials. Match quality to use; avoid contaminating potable plumbing. Maintain and test systems. Prefer safer supplies for ingestion and food uses; debris diversion does not alone make rain potable.

record.title: 12VAC5-635-240 Design and installation
record.locator: Subsections G-I
record.finding: Regulated systems require prefiltration, an automatic accessible first-flush device after prefiltration, protected storage openings and defined inlet/outlet arrangements. This section does not prescribe the book's four-inch diversion quantity. Applicability and rain-barrel exclusions must be assessed separately.

record.title: Rainwater Harvesting
record.locator: BIG PICTURE; non-potable and POTABLE use questions
record.finding: Virginia permits regulated potable rainwater systems under Tier 4 construction and operating approvals. Rain barrels are excluded from the regulations. Other new nonpotable systems have registration obligations, and building/local rules still apply. No general tax-credit entitlement is established by this page.

record.title: 12VAC5-630-410 Construction; general
record.locator: B Well bore; C Casing; D Screens; F Grouting
record.finding: Well design depends on geology. Casing protects bore and water quality; screen dimensions depend on formation analysis. Private wells require grouting, with class-specific casing and completion requirements. A bag and uncontrolled mud backfill are not demonstrated compliance.

record.title: 13VAC5-63-210: residential nonpotable gray water provisions
record.locator: P2910 and P2911 amendments, especially P2911.1.1, .2, .4 and .6
record.finding: Graywater systems need separation from potable plumbing, use-specific quality and filtration/disinfection where required, approved bypass and backwater provisions. Untreated graywater tank retention is limited to 24 hours. Building plumbing approval does not remove VDH/DEQ responsibilities for treatment and discharge.

record.title: How Do Hydrologists Locate Groundwater?
record.locator: Locating groundwater
record.finding: Groundwater occupies pores and cracks in soils and rocks. Hydrogeologic maps, nearby well records, testing and chemical analysis inform quantity and quality. Valleys and water-loving plants may offer clues, without guaranteeing usable water. Neither fixed drilling depth nor surface clues replace investigation.

record.title: Household Water Treatment
record.locator: Slow sand filtration
record.finding: Designed slow-sand treatment includes fine sand, support gravel, underdrains and regulated flow. This description does not validate the book's gravel-sand-carbon bucket design as a pathogen barrier.

record.title: 12VAC5-630-220 Permits and inspection statement
record.locator: A-C
record.finding: Private wells must meet regulations; construction, alteration, deepening and abandonment require written permission, with stated exceptions. Operation generally requires an inspection statement. Emergency or DIY intent does not itself create an exemption.

record.title: 12VAC5-630-431 Water quality
record.locator: A-F
record.finding: Class III drinking-water wells require disinfection and bacteriological examination by an accredited laboratory under specified interpretation rules. Class IV nonconsumption wells are exempt from this section's water-quality requirements; a negative coliform result is not a complete chemical screen.

record.title: Water Dowsing
record.locator: What does science say about dowsing?
record.finding: Apparent dowsing success can reflect widespread groundwater; scientific location of depth, quantity and quality requires hydrologic, geologic and geophysical investigation.

record.title: Discussion on Humidity
record.locator: Relative humidity discussion
record.finding: Warm air can contain more vapor; with unchanged moisture, warming reduces relative humidity and cooling raises it. Dew point better represents actual moisture content than relative humidity alone.

record.title: Fix a Leak Week
record.locator: Checking for Leaks; Toilet Leaks; Faucet Leaks
record.finding: Inspect for household leaks and repair faulty fixtures and seals to conserve water; the specific cause of a leak requires diagnosis.

record.title: Potable Water Reuse and Drinking Water
record.locator: Direct and indirect reuse
record.finding: Potable reuse requires treatment within drinking-water and water-quality protections. Indirect reuse includes an environmental buffer before drinking-water treatment. Ordinary wastewater discharge and validated potable reuse are different treatment endpoints.

record.title: Bleach treatment
record.guidance: Use the concentration-specific EPA table; for clear water use eight drops of 6% or six of 8.25% bleach per gallon. Double for cloudy, colored or very cold water after settling/prefiltration; wait 30 minutes. If no slight chlorine odor, repeat dose and wait 15 more minutes. Do not infer precise milliliters from an arbitrary dropper.

record.title: Calcium hypochlorite
record.guidance: EPA describes a heaping teaspoon of high-test calcium hypochlorite in two gallons to make stock, then one part stock to 100 parts water (one pint per 12.5 gallons). Follow product suitability and oxidizer precautions; do not adopt the book’s inconsistent ounce-per-three-quarts shortcut.

record.title: Iodine limits
record.guidance: Use only a defined product and label protocol. CDC cautions against iodine for pregnancy, thyroid conditions or iodine hypersensitivity and use beyond a few weeks. Do not rely on iodine for all parasites; it is not the default household long-term treatment.

record.title: Emergency boiling
record.guidance: Use CDC’s rolling boil: one minute, or three minutes above 6,500 feet, then cool and protect from recontamination. This controls germs and does not remove chemical hazards. EPA’s displayed altitude threshold differs (5,000 feet and an inconsistent metric equivalent); this dataset explicitly adopts CDC’s threshold, with local health instructions taking precedence.

record.title: Container sanitation and storage
record.guidance: Use CDC’s wash/sanitize/fill/close method and six-month replacement interval for home-filled water. A sealed lid and one bleach dose do not establish indefinite safe storage. Keep container sanitation solution separate from drinking-water dosing.

record.title: Pools are nonpotable reserves
record.guidance: Use pool water only for appropriate non-drinking purposes; normal pool maintenance does not make a drinking-water supply.

record.title: Rainfall arithmetic and reliability
record.guidance: US liquid gallon is 231 cubic inches: gallons = horizontal square feet × rainfall inches × 144 / 231. Thus 850 × 23 gives 12,187.012987 gallons/year, 33.389077/day gross; 2,000 × 23 gives 28,675.324675/year. The book’s 6,452-gallon reference is inconsistent. Subtract first flush, collection losses and overflow and model dry periods; annual yield divided by 365 is not dependable daily supply.

record.title: Virginia rainwater law
record.guidance: Virginia allows potable rainwater under Tier 4 requirements. Check system applicability, construction and operation permits, testing and building/local requirements. The reviewed design rule requires first flush but does not state four inches; the claimed general tax credit was not substantiated and remains unresolved.

record.title: Well sanitary completion
record.guidance: Use an approved class-specific casing, screen, grout and wellhead design; a buried plastic bag and tamped mud do not establish sanitary protection. Required testing and inspection still apply.

record.title: Dowsing
record.guidance: Use hydrogeologic investigation and testing. Do not rely on crossing rods to establish groundwater depth, quantity or quality.

record.title: Relative humidity
record.guidance: At fixed vapor content, warming lowers relative humidity and cooling raises it. Dew requires an adequately cold surface; fog interception is a separate mechanism. Neither high relative humidity alone nor morning sunlight establishes harvest yield.

record.title: Greywater controls
record.guidance: Treat greywater as potentially contaminated. Use approved separate systems and use-specific treatment, bypass and backflow protections; Virginia’s cited residential provisions limit untreated tank storage to 24 hours. Do not use untreated shower water for dishes or treat any outdoor discharge as automatically lawful.

record.title: Potable reuse
record.guidance: Potable reuse needs purpose-designed treatment, monitoring and applicable approvals. Conventional wastewater effluent and household distilled urine are not established safe drinking-water sources by these descriptions.
